exact.e: From Latin exāctus (the verb via Middle English exact), perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due; measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).
exact.g: Precisely agreeing with a standard, a fact, or the truth; perfectly conforming; neither exceeding nor falling short in any respect.

exaction.e: From Middle English exaccioun, exaccion, from Middle French exaction, from Old French, from Latin exāctiō.
exaction.g: The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay or yield; compulsion to give or furnish; a levying by force

exalt.e: From Middle English exalten, from Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō.
exalt.g: To honor; to hold in high esteem; to praise or worship.

exaltation.e: From Middle English exaltacioun, exaltatioun, from Old French exaltacion and Latin exaltātiō (“exaltation, elevation”), from exaltō (“raise, elevate, exalt”), from ex (“from, out of”) + altus (“high”). By surface analysis, exalt + -ation.
exaltation.g: The act of exalting or raising high; also, the state of being exalted; elevation.

examination.e: From Middle English examinacioun, from Old French examinacion, from Latin exāminātiō. Morphologically examine + -ation.

examine.e: From Middle English examinen, examenen, from Old French examiner, from Latin exāmināre.
examine.g: To observe carefully or critically to learn about someone or something.

example.e: From Middle English example, exaumple, from Old French example, essaumple, from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”, literally “what is taken out”); see exempt.
example.g: Something that is representative of all such things in a group.

exceed.e: From Middle English exceden, from Old French exceder, from Latin excēdō (“to go beyond”), from ex- (“out, forth”) with cēdō (“to go”); see cede and compare accede etc. Partly displaced native Old English ofersteppan, whence Modern English overstep.

excel.e: From Middle English excellen, from Old French exceller, from Latin excellere, excelsum; ex (“out”) + *cellō, an unattested verb root found in culmen (“height, top”);.
excel.g: To surpass someone or something; to be better or do better than someone or something.

excellence.e: From Middle English excellence, from Old French excellence, from Latin excellentia.
excellence.g: The quality of being excellent; brilliance

excellency.e: From Middle English excellencie, from Latin excellentia.
excellency.g: Synonym of excellence; the quality of being excellent.

excellent.e: From Middle English excellent, from Old French excellent, from Latin excellēns (“elevated, exalted”), present participle of excellō (“elevate, exult”), equivalent to excel + -ent.

except.e: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.
except.g: To exclude; to specify as being an exception.

exception.e: From Middle English exception, excepcioun, from Anglo-Norman excepcioun, from Old French excepcion, from Latin exceptiō. Equivalent to except + -ion.
exception.g: The act of excepting or excluding; exclusion; restriction by taking out something which would otherwise be included, as in a class, statemen

excess.e: From Middle English exces (“excess, ecstasy”), from Old French exces, from Latin excessus (“a going out, loss of self-possession”), from excedere, excessum (“to go out, go beyond”).
excess.g: The state of surpassing or going beyond a limit; the state of being beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; more than what is usual or prope

excessive.e: From Middle English excessive, excessif, from Old French excessif, from Medieval Latin excessivus, equivalent to excess + -ive.
excessive.g: Exceeding the usual bounds of something; too much (of amount); extravagant; immoderate.

exchange.e: From Middle English eschaunge, borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschaunge, from Old French eschange (whence modern French échange), from the verb eschanger, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō). Spelling later changed on the basis of ex-, with pronunciation following. By surface analysis, ex- + change.
exchange.g: An act of exchanging or trading.

exchange.e: From Middle English eschaungen, from Anglo-Norman eschaungier, Old French eschanger, from the Old French verb eschangier, eschanger (whence modern French échanger), from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō).

exchanger.g: A person or thing that exchanges one thing for another.

excitement.e: From Middle English excitement, from Old French excitement, equivalent to excite + -ment.
excitement.g: The state of being excited (emotionally aroused).

exclaim.e: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).
exclaim.g: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.

exclude.e: Borrowed from Latin exclūdō, from prefix ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudō (“close”).
exclude.g: To bar (someone or something) from entering; to keep out.

exclusively.e: From Middle English exclusyvely; equivalent to exclusive + -ly.
exclusively.g: To the exclusion of anything or anyone else; solely or entirely.

excrement.e: Borrowed from Latin excrēmentum, from excernō (“to excrete”).
excrement.g: Human and non-human animal solid waste excreted from the bowels; feces.

excrement.e: Borrowed from Latin excrēmentum, from excrēscō (“to grow out”).
excrement.g: Something which grows out of the body; hair, nails, etc.

excuse.e: From Middle English excusen (verb) and excuse (noun), borrowed from Old French escuser (verb) and excuse (noun), from Latin excūsō, excūsāre (“to excuse, allege in excuse, literally, free from a charge”), from ex (“out”) + causa (“a charge”); see cause, accuse and recuse.
excuse.g: To forgive; to pardon; to overlook.

execration.g: An act or instance of cursing; a curse dictated by violent feelings of hatred; an imprecation; an expression of utter detestation.

execute.e: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).
execute.g: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.

execution.e: From Old French execution (c.1360), from Latin exsecutiō, an agent noun from exsequor (“to follow out”), from ex (“out”) + sequor (“follow”). Equivalent to execute + -ion.
execution.g: The act, manner or style of executing (actions, maneuvers, performances).

executor.e: From Middle English executour, from Anglo-Norman executour, from Latin exsecūtor, agent noun of exsequor.
executor.g: A person who carries out some task.

exempt.e: From Middle French exempt, from Latin exemptus, past participle of eximō.
exempt.g: Free from a duty, obligation, rule, law, etc.

exercise.e: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium.
exercise.g: Any activity designed to develop or hone a skill or ability.

exert.e: From Latin exsertus, past participle of exserō (“to stretch or thrust forth or out”), from ex- + serō (“to string together”).
exert.g: To make use of, to apply, especially of something nonmaterial; to bring to bear.

exhaust.e: From Latin exhaustus, past participle of exhaurīre (“to draw out, drink up, empty, exhaust”), from ex (“out”) + haurīre (“to draw (especially water), drain”).
exhaust.g: To draw or let out wholly; to drain completely.

exhaustion.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustiō, from exhauriō. Surface analysis: exhaust + -ion.
exhaustion.g: The point of complete depletion, of the state of being used up.

exhort.e: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

exhortation.e: From Middle English exhortacioun, from Old French exhortacion, from Latin exhortātiōnem, accusative singular of exhortātiō (“encouraging; exhortation”), from exhortor (“to encourage, exhort”), from ex (“out of, from”) + hortor (“encourage”). By surface analysis, exhort + -ation.
exhortation.g: The act or practice of exhorting.

exile.e: From Middle English exil, borrowed from Old French essil, exil, from Latin exsilium, exilium (“state of exile”), derived from exsul, exul (“exiled person”).
exile.g: The state of being banished from one's home or country.

exist.e: From French exister, from Latin existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist, appear, arise”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (“stand”); see stand.
exist.g: to be; have existence; have being or reality

exit.e: From Middle English exit, from Latin exitus (“departure, going out; way by which one may go out, egress; (figuratively) conclusion, termination; (figuratively) death; income, revenue”), from exeō (“to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns from verbs).
exit.g: An act of going out or going away, or leaving; a departure.

exit.e: Borrowed from Latin exit, the third-person singular present active indicative of exeō (“to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”); see further at etymology 1 above.
exit.g: Used as a stage direction for an actor: to leave the scene or stage.

exodus.e: From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, procession, departure”). From late Old English only as a proper noun, Exodus, the biblical book; use as a common noun is from the early 17th century.
exodus.g: A sudden departure of a large number of people.

exorcist.e: From Middle French exorciste, from Latin exorcista, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκιστής (exorkistḗs).
exorcist.g: A person, especially a priest or priestess, who is a practitioner in exorcism to force out evil spirits or demons from a living being.

exotic.e: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”).
exotic.g: Foreign, especially in an exciting way.

expand.e: Recorded in Middle English since 1422 (as expanden, expaunden), from Anglo-Norman espaundre, from Latin expandō (“to spread out”), itself from ex- (“out, outwards”) + pandō (“to spread”).
expand.g: To change (something) from a smaller form or size to a larger one; to spread out or lay open.

expanse.g: A wide stretch, usually of sea, sky, or land.

expect.e: From Latin expectāre, infinitive form of exspectō (“look out for, await, expect”), from ex (“out”) + spectō (“look at”), frequentative of speciō (“see”).
expect.g: To predict or believe that something will happen

expectant.e: From Old French expectant, from Latin expectans.

expectation.e: From Middle French expectation, from Latin exspectātiō, from exspectō (“expect”). By surface analysis, expect + -ation.
expectation.g: The act or state of expecting or looking forward to an event as about to happen.

expedient.e: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).
expedient.g: Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.

expel.e: Late Middle English: from Latin expellere, from ex- (“out”) + pellere (“to drive”).

expend.e: Borrowed from Latin expendō (“to weigh; to pay out”).

expense.e: From Middle English expense, from Anglo-Norman expense and Old French espense, from Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expendō.
expense.g: A spending or consuming, often a disbursement of funds.

expensive.e: From Latin *expēnsīvus, from expendō (“to weigh out (money), to pay out”) (whence English expend). By surface analysis, expense + -ive.
expensive.g: Having a high price or cost.

experience.e: From Middle English experience, from Old French, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens, present participle of experiri (“to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (“out”) + peritus (“experienced, expert”), past participle of *periri (“to go through”); see expert and peril.
experience.g: The effect upon the judgment or feelings produced by any event, whether witnessed or participated in; personal and direct impressions as con

experiment.e: From Middle English experiment, from Old French esperiment (French expérience), from Latin experimentum (“experience, attempt, experiment”), from experior (“to experience, to attempt”), itself from ex + *perior, in turn from Proto-Indo-European *per-.
experiment.g: A test under controlled conditions made to either demonstrate a known truth, examine the validity of a hypothesis, or determine the efficacy

expert.e: From Middle English expert, derived from Old French expert (“experienced”), espert, from Latin expertus (contracted from *experitus), perfect active participle of experior (“to try”), from ex- + *-perior.

expire.e: From Middle English expire, from Middle French expirer, from Latin expīrō, exspīrō, from ex- (“out”) + spīrō (“breathe, be alive”).

explain.e: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”); see plain and plane.
explain.g: To make plain, manifest, or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to illustrate the meaning of.

explanation.e: From Latin explanatio (“an explanation, interpretation”), from explanare (“explain”); see explain. Morphologically explain + -ation.
explanation.g: The act or process of explaining.

explore.e: From Middle French explorer, from Latin explōrāre (“to investigate, search out”), itself said to be originally a hunters' term meaning "to set up a loud cry", from ex- (“out”) + plōrāre (“to cry”), but the second element is also explained as "to make to flow" (from pluere (“to flow”)).
explore.g: To seek for something or after someone.

export.g: Of or relating to exportation or exports.

expose.e: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”).
expose.g: To reveal; to uncover; to make visible; to bring to light.

expound.e: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere.
expound.g: To set out the meaning of; to explain or discuss at length.

express.e: From French exprès, from Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (see Etymology 2, below).
express.g: Moving or operating quickly, as a train not making local stops.

express.e: From Old French espresser, expresser, from frequentative form of Latin exprimere.
express.g: To convey or communicate; to make known or explicit.

expression.e: Borrowed from Middle French expression, from Late Latin expressiō, expressiōnem (“a pressing out”). Morphologically express + -ion.
expression.g: The action of expressing thoughts, ideas, feelings, etc.

extend.e: From Middle English extenden, from Anglo-Norman extendre, estendre, from Latin extendō (“to stretch out”).

extension.e: From Middle English extensioun, from Old French estension, from Latin extensiō, extensiōnem.
extension.g: The act of extending; a stretching out; enlargement in length, breadth, or time; an increase.

extensive.e: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin extensīvus, from Latin extensus.
extensive.g: Having a great extent; covering a large area; vast.

extent.e: From Middle English extente, from Anglo-Norman extente and Old French estente (“valuation of land, stretch of land”), from estendre, extendre (“extend”) (or from Latin extentus), from Latin extendere (See extend.)
extent.g: A range of values or locations.

exterminate.e: Borrowed from Latin exterminātus, perfect passive participle of exterminō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“thoroughly”) + terminō (“to finish, close, end”), from terminus (“limit, end”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).
exterminate.g: To kill or otherwise permanently eliminate all of (a population, often of pests or undesirables), usually intentionally.

extermination.e: Borrowed from Middle French extermination, itself a learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin exterminātiō.
extermination.g: The act of exterminating; total destruction or eradication.

external.e: From Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin externus (“outward, external”), from exter/exterus (“on the outside, outward”).
external.g: Outside of something; on the exterior.

extinct.e: From Late Middle English extinct (“eliminated, eradicated, extinguished”), from Latin extīnctus, exstīnctus (“extinguished, quenched; destroyed, killed; made extinct”), the perfect passive participles of extinguō, exstinguō (“to extinguish, put out, quench; (figurative) to abolish; to destroy, kill”), from ex- (prefix meaning ‘away.
extinct.g: Of fire, etc.: no longer alight; of a light, etc.: no longer shining; extinguished, quenched.

extinct.e: From Middle English extincten (“to extinguish or put out (a fire, light, etc.); to destroy, kill; (figurative) to suppress (an uprising); (law) to quash or stop (legal proceedings); to cancel (a privilege, title, etc.); (medicine) to eliminate or reduce (inflammation, an ulcer, etc.)”).

extinguish.e: Borrowed from Latin extinguo (“to put out (what is burning), quench, extinguish, deprive of life, destroy, abolish”), from ex (“out”) + stinguere (“to put out, quench, extinguish”).

extol.e: Borrowed from Latin extollō (“elevate, raise high”).

extort.e: Borrowed from Latin extortus, past participle of extorquere (“to twist or wrench out, to extort”); from ex (“out”) + -tort, from torqueō (“twist, turn”).
extort.g: To take or seize from an unwilling person by physical force, menace, duress, torture, or any undue or illegal exercise of power or ingenuity

extortion.e: From Middle English extorcion, from Anglo-Norman extorcion, extorcioun, extorsioun, from Late Latin extortiō, from extorqueō. By surface analysis, extort + -ion.
extortion.g: The practice of extorting money or other property by the use of force or threats.

extraordinary.e: From Latin extrāōrdinārius. By surface analysis, extra- + ordinary.
extraordinary.g: Out of the ordinary; exceptional; unusual.

extravagance.e: Borrowed from French extravagance, from Medieval Latin extra + vagor (“to wander”).
extravagance.g: Excessive or superfluous expenditure of money.

extreme.e: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French extreme, from Latin extrēmus, the superlative of exter.
extreme.g: Of a place, the most remote, farthest or outermost.

extremity.e: From Middle English extremite, from Old French extremité, from Latin extrēmitātem (“extremity; border, perimeter; ending”), from extrēmīs (“furthest, extreme”) + -itās (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being); see extreme.
extremity.g: The most extreme or furthest point of something.

exult.e: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).
exult.g: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).

exultation.e: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.
exultation.g: The act of exulting; great joy at success or victory, or at any advantage gained; rapturous delight
